Week 12 Data Reuse Project · Arabidopsis transcriptomics

Shared WRKY75-associated genes in nitrogen response and leaf senescence

Reanalysis of GEO GSE184528 and GSE102302 asks which genes respond differently to high nitrogen in wrky75 roots and also appear in a published WRKY75 RNAi leaf comparison.

12 root RNA-seq libraries2 independent studiesFactorial DESeq2 reanalysis
SummaryData and methodsNitrogen responseCross-study overlapBiological processesInterpretationReproducibility

01 · Abstract

A shared set of candidate genes

The nitrogen response depended on WRKY75 genotype for 1,709 genes at a 5% false discovery rate. Of those, 194 also appeared in published WRKY75 RNAi leaf lists. The overlap identifies candidates for follow-up across tissues and conditions. A cross-study enrichment P-value could not be calculated because the complete tested-gene universe was unavailable for the leaf study.

1,709Significant genotype × nitrogen interactions
194Also listed in the leaf study
163Enriched GO Biological Process terms in the nitrogen interaction set

02 · Data and methods

Two studies, two distinct comparisons

Nitrogen response. GSE184528 experiment 2 profiled roots of seven-day-old Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings after two hours with or without 20 mM NH4NO3 at pH 5.8. The twelve matched GEO accessions make a balanced Col-0 / wrky75 × control / high N design with three biological replicates per combination. The five wrky40 libraries and experiment 1 (Col-0 / agb1-2) were excluded by design. Control is the study baseline without added high nitrogen. [1]

Leaf senescence. GSE102302 profiled the third and fourth leaves of 28-day-old Col-0 and WRKY75 RNAi plants, with one deposited library per condition. This project reused the authors’ upregulated and downregulated lists and did not test differential expression from these two libraries. The lists capture associations with RNAi in a senescence study; they do not isolate a senescence time effect or prove direct transcriptional regulation. [2]

The two count workbooks each have one worksheet and 34,218 unique original feature identifiers. All count cells are nonnegative integers. Experiment 2 contains 17 sample columns and experiment 1 contains 12. The experiment 2 IDs include 32,833 AGI-pattern IDs and 1,385 other identifiers, including ENSRNA IDs. All original count IDs were preserved for modeling; exact AGI locus matching was used for cross-study analysis and annotation.

Factorial model and contrasts

The count matrix was filtered to features with at least 10 reads in at least three selected samples, retaining 20,264 of 34,218 features. DESeq2 fitted a negative binomial model with median-ratio size factors and the design ~ genotype * nitrogen. Col-0 and control were reference levels. The primary Wald test was the interaction; secondary contrasts estimated treatment within genotype and genotype within treatment. P-values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg separately for each contrast, with DESeq2 independent filtering at α = 0.05. Reported log2 fold changes are unshrunken. No additional fold-change cutoff was imposed. [3]

Interaction = (wrky75 high N − wrky75 control) − (Col-0 high N − Col-0 control), on the log2 scale. A positive value means a more positive high-N response in the mutant; the gene can still decrease in both genotypes.

03 · Root RNA-seq

High nitrogen separates the samples, with a replicate-order pattern

Assigned counts ranged from 17.77 to 21.43 million per selected library. On the 500 most variable variance-stabilized features, PC1 (63.3%) shifted in the same direction under high N within both genotypes. PC2 (20.5%) tracked replicate number within all 4 groups. Because GEO does not establish a matched block from replicate labels, the primary fit kept the factorial design and retained all 12 samples. A sensitivity fit included replicate index as an exploratory covariate.

The wild type had more significant high-N responses than the mutant (4,548 versus 3,008). Comparing two significance counts alone does not establish a genotype difference. The interaction directly tests that question and identified 760 more positive and 949 less positive high-N responses in wrky75 relative to Col-0.

Replicate-index sensitivity. The exploratory fit found 2,072 significant interactions, with 1,571 significant in both fits and 1,571 of those agreeing in sign. Interaction estimates correlated at r = 0.972. Of the 194 primary shared candidates, 183 also met the interaction threshold in the sensitivity fit. The choice of model changes which genes pass the cutoff; the overlap is not confined to a single fit.

04 · Cross-study comparison

194 interaction genes are also in the leaf lists

After uppercasing identifiers and stripping terminal transcript suffixes such as .1, 1,360 upregulated rows mapped to 1,231 loci, and 998 downregulated rows mapped to 931 loci after excluding the unresolvable numeric ID 8. Three loci appeared in both lists after collapse (AT2G24250, AT5G15790, AT5G47455); each was counted once in the union of 2,159 genes. Published rows, including transcript suffixes and conflicting directions, remain in the audit tables. An extra down-workbook worksheet contains previously computed GO output; two extra worksheets in the up workbook are empty. Neither was treated as a gene list.

The primary intersection contained 128 loci listed as upregulated in RNAi leaves and 66 listed as downregulated (11.4% of significant interactions). The published leaf log fold change and the root interaction are different quantities, so their signs cannot be interpreted as replication of the same effect.

No cross-study enrichment test. The GEO supplements provide selected leaf hits, but no complete list of genes that were eligible for detection and testing in that study. A genome-wide background, the published hit union, or the nitrogen-only tested set would not be a defensible common universe. The overlap has no enrichment P-value or claim of excess over chance.

05 · Functional enrichment

Nutrient response and stress-related processes are over-represented

GO Biological Process analysis tested the nitrogen interaction set on its own. 1,284 significant AGI loci had BP annotations among 14,580 annotated genes with an adjusted interaction P-value. We used the Arabidopsis annotation database org.At.tair.db and propagated GO BP annotations (GOALL), retaining terms with 10–500 background genes. A one-sided hypergeometric test and BH adjustment across all 2,177 eligible terms identified 163 terms at FDR < 0.05. No GO test was reported for the cross-study intersection because its common sampling universe was unavailable. [4]

The top term was response to nutrient levels (58 genes, 2.57× enrichment, FDR 2.55e-08). Several related oxygen-response terms were also prominent, alongside carbohydrate biosynthesis and secondary metabolism. Related GO terms share annotations; oxygen-response enrichment does not show that these roots experienced hypoxia.

06 · Discussion

The overlap narrows the search for a shared program

The new question here is whether a WRKY75-dependent response to an acute nitrogen perturbation in roots shares genes with a WRKY75-associated expression signature in mature leaves. The 194 candidates show that these two sets intersect. The GO results suggest that WRKY75 genotype alters expression of genes involved in nutrient response and broader stress-related processes in the root experiment. The overlap and GO results address different questions, and neither establishes a causal link between high nitrogen and leaf senescence.

Two shared loci illustrate distinct response patterns. The class 1 phytoglobin locus AT2G16060 (PGB1) decreased under high N in both root genotypes, but less strongly in wrky75 (log2 fold change -4.60 in Col-0 versus -1.93 in the mutant). The peptide transporter locus AT3G54140 (PTR1/NPF8.1) increased in both, but less strongly in wrky75 (2.11 versus 0.63). Both appeared in the leaf RNAi lists. These loci are candidates for asking how nitrogen and oxygen-related responses intersect with WRKY75-associated leaf expression. [4]

Limitations. The studies differ in tissue, plant age, perturbation (mutant versus RNAi), and sequencing and analysis pipelines. The senescence data have no replicate-based estimate of variability in the deposited contrast. The selected leaf lists omit non-hits and therefore cannot support an overlap enrichment test. In the root study, three replicates per group limit precision, and the PC2 pattern raises the possibility of a technical or sampling gradient not specified in GEO. GO annotation coverage and gene detectability affect over-representation estimates; GO terms are correlated and should be read as groups of related functions.

Next steps. Retrieve the complete original leaf differential-expression table and identify loci eligible for testing in both experiments before testing overlap. Prioritize shared genes that retain their interaction in the sensitivity fit. Replicated experiments measuring root and leaf expression under matched nitrogen treatments and developmental stages could distinguish tissue specificity from a shared response. A binding assay and complementation would help separate direct WRKY75 regulation from downstream effects.

07 · Reproducibility

Trace every result to its input

The workflow uses R 4.4.1, DESeq2 1.44.0 and Arabidopsis/GO annotations from Bioconductor 3.19. The project includes the validation script, R analysis and sensitivity scripts, raw file hashes, result tables, and session information. The scripts verify all 12 sample assignments and nonnegative integer counts, check the design rank, reconstruct interaction estimates from both pairs of simple contrasts, independently recalculate BH and GO results, and confirm the gene intersection. The two contrast identity errors were below 10−8.
